topics: FP8 accuracy variation on attention vs MLP layers
KV cache evictions and sticky sessions
On-prem VPC constraints and KMS impacts
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Okay, thanks everyone for joining, we'll run through the regression traces and then get into per-layer fallback ideas. Nora, Ethan, can you hear us?
[00:22] Nora: Yep, loud and clear. We've been seeing a small but consistent token drift after we flipped AWQ plus FP8 in staging, it's subtle but reproducible across corpora.
[00:45] Priya: To set context: two axes here - quantization algorithm (AWQ vs GPTQ) and runtime execution precision (FP8 path vs INT8/FP16). Sometimes the runtime will select a faster FP8 kernel which introduces rounding differences.
[01:10] Ethan: Pattern: higher regressions on longer-context prompts and when our KV cache hit rate dips <70%. That suggests eviction/prefetch interactions.
[01:35] Liam: Also we saw the MLP dense layers are more sensitive in our microbenchmarks; attention projection layers are sometimes robust to AWQ. The FP8 kernels use different scaling heuristics and stochastic rounding—which can amplify layerwise drift.
[01:58] Nora: When you say layerwise, can you point to which layers to prioritize for fallback? We can't flip everything to fp16 because of latency SLOs.
[02:22] Priya: Two approaches: static manifests (compile-time: mark layers as no-quant) or dynamic runtime gating that flips precision based on token-delta thresholds. Static is simpler and less risky for on-prem. Dynamic gives more headroom but requires careful KV handling.
[02:50] Samir: Dynamic gating sounds attractive but how quickly can it flip without trashing the KV cache and causing p99 spikes?
[03:15] Priya: Flipping a layer's precision mid-session changes the KV representation and typically requires invalidating that layer's KV entries, which forces prefix recomputation. For low-latency chat, that's bad. So we recommend dynamic flips only at request boundaries or only for ephemeral batch jobs, not long-lived sessions.
[03:42] Maya: That's rough for our chat use case. We've seen tail-latency spikes when cache misses happen mid-session.
[04:05] Jordan: Proposal: run offline per-layer sensitivity eval, produce a fallback manifest marking top-3 sensitive layers as FP16, keep remaining AWQ/FP8, then deploy a canary with KV-sticky sessions so the canary doesn't thrash the shared cache.
[04:35] Nora: OK, but we need concrete numbers: accuracy delta vs latency delta per-layer. Samir, can you run layer-swap ablations on the 5k prompt set?
[04:58] Samir: Yes. Do you want token-level cross-entropy diffs or aggregate BLEU/ROUGE style metrics?
[05:20] Priya: Both. Token diffs for debugging, aggregate metrics for decisioning. Also collect p50/p95/p99 latencies and tail-percentile QPS under batching.
[05:45] Ethan: On infra: our Dedicated profile in-prem uses fixed GPU pools and we have limited batching headroom. If enabling FP16 on a layer raises memory by X it might reduce batch size and hurt throughput; we need to model that tradeoff.
[06:10] Liam: We'll run microbenchmarks that report per-layer memory delta and per-token latency delta with different batch sizes. We'll include KV-sticky vs KV-evict runs.
[06:35] Nora: We also want visibility to token-level diffs aligned with user intents. Some diffs are benign word swaps, others are hallucinations. Is there tooling to flag semantic regressions?
[07:00] Priya: Redwood's eval harness can produce token diffs plus an approximate semantic-change score using embeddings distance on outputs. We'll include that in the export.
[07:22] Samir: A note on AWQ vs GPTQ: in our prior experiments GPTQ produced slightly better fidelity on some layers but slower quant/deploy times. AWQ is faster to generate but can have heavier per-layer variance. We'll capture both.
[07:50] Jordan: On rollback criteria: agree that a canary fails if token-level shift exceeds threshold on 0.5% of prompts or if p99 latency increases by >30% for canary traffic. Also auto-rollback if error rate increases by 2x.
[08:12] Maya: KMS note: on-prem VPC KMS policies mean we can't upload certain compiled manifests to a shared control plane unless signed. We'll need an option to store manifests locally or use a signed artifact exchange.
[08:35] Priya: Good call—Redwood can provide a signed manifest artifact and a verification script so Orchard can validate locally.
[08:50] Ethan: About KV sticky sessions: we need a routing cookie that maps sessions to a canary shard and keeps their KV affinity. Can Redwood expose sticky session headers in the API?
[09:10] Jordan: Yes, we have a session-affinity header and a canary token split config. We'll share config examples.
[09:25] Nora: Halfway through, can you summarize the eval matrices you'll provide?
[09:35] Priya: We'll deliver: (1) Per-layer sensitivity table AWQ vs GPTQ vs baseline fp16, with token-diff stats and latency delta; (2) Microbenchmarks for FP8/INT8 kernels across typical seq lengths and batch sizes; (3) Manifest generator that picks top-k layers to exclude; (4) Canary config with sticky-session example.
[10:05] Samir: For the per-layer tests, I'll run three variants: base FP16, full AWQ/FP8, and hybrid manifests where selected layers are FP16. We'll log token diffs and semantic distance.
[10:30] Liam: We'll also supply a lightweight bisection tool that can take a seed set and binary-search to find the first layer where drift exceeds threshold—helps produce the fallback manifest faster.
[10:50] Nora: How many layers do you usually end up excluding in practice?
[11:00] Priya: Typically 1-5 layers for large decoders; often the final MLP and one middle attention projection are the culprits. But it varies by model and dataset.
[11:20] Ethan: Can the compile step emit per-layer checksums so we can detect if model weights changed during transfer? We need artifact integrity checks for compliance.
[11:34] Jordan: Yes, the manifest will include weight checksums, quant seed, compiler flags, and the matrix of microbenchmarks.
[11:50] Maya: Anything on rollout scheduling? We prefer a 2-week canary with 10% traffic and daily snapshot diffs. If daily diffs exceed thresholds we'll pause and bisect.
[12:10] Jordan: Agreed. We'll provide a canary runbook that covers traffic split, sticky-session config, rollback triggers, and how to run the bisection tool on diff spikes.
[12:32] Samir: One more question: in-staging we saw non-deterministic diffs between runs. Are we confident that's quantization nondeterminism and not RNG or prompt normalization?
[12:50] Liam: We instrumented seeds and RNG paths; the noise correlates with kernel selection and FP8 stochastic rounding. Deterministic modes exist but cost latency. We'll quantify that too.
[13:15] Nora: Good. Let's talk timing: can Redwood provide the manifests and microbenchmarks by EOD Monday?
[13:28] Jordan: We'll aim for end-of-day Monday, plus the bisection tool and canary runbook. Priya will attach the signed manifest workflow.
[13:45] Priya: I'll also include examples for on-prem verification and the header for session-affinity.
[14:00] Ethan: For our part we'll prepare the eval set and an infra window to run dedicated-profile tests next week.
[14:15] Nora: Great. Anything else on KV edge cases? One edge case: cached prefixes from earlier model versions have a different tokenization mapping; can we detect and reject mismatched KV during startup?
[14:35] Priya: Yes the manifest validator checks tokenization hash and kv-version. If mismatched, the runtime can either reject requests or fall back to cold-start prefix regeneration—configurable.
[14:50] Samir: OK I'll include a set of intentional mismatch tests to verify the validator behavior.
[15:05] Jordan: Alright let's capture next steps and action owners. Thanks everyone.
[15:20] Nora: Thanks all.
[15:30] Jordan: Meeting adjourned.
